source.title: Position: Solve Layerwise Linear Models First to Understand Neural Dynamical Phenomena (Neural Collapse, Emergence, Lazy/Rich Regime, and Grokking)
source.authors: Yoonsoo Nam; S. Lee; C. Dominé; Yeachan Park; Charles London; W. Choi; N. Göring; Seungjai Lee

record.file_problem: Minor garbling in Figure 6 labels; the relevant Figure 8 text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports an experiment on MNIST, a non-algorithmic image dataset, and varies initialization and scaling settings to examine delayed generalization.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own MNIST MLP experiment in Figure 8 and explicitly describes the default setting as grokking and the modified settings as eliminating the delay. Other discussion of grokking, including algorithmic-task results and large-model settings, is attributed to cited work and is not recorded as results here. Figure 6 examines NTK change on randomized regression, not delayed generalization, so it is not a row.
record.test_reason: In its own experiment (Fig. 8, App. G.3), a 4-layer tanh MLP on 1000 MNIST samples with 5× initialization shows delayed generalization. Four changes that lower the weight-to-target ratio (weight downscaling, target upscaling, input downscaling, output downscaling) remove the delay. This bears on V3 (non-algorithmic data; delay switched by initialization and scale) in a setting new relative to the originals. Everything else in this position paper is review of cited work or theory.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. In this position paper, the authors argue that layerwise linear models and the 'dynamical feedback principle' explain grokking as a delayed escape from a lazy regime caused by a large weight-to-target ratio. Their MNIST MLP experiment shows that reducing this ratio by any of four scalings removes the generalization delay. They present this as confirmation of Kumar et al. (2024) rather than a new discovery.
record.recipe_differences: The empirical experiment uses a four-layer tanh MLP on flattened MNIST with scaling and initialization changes, rather than the original small algorithmic-dataset setup. The paper also reviews cited work but those results are not its own experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported delay changes with weight initialization ratio, target scale, input scale, and output scale.

fits_no_version.finding: In linear funnel and anti-funnel networks on randomized regression, extreme layer imbalance first gives lazy dynamics and then a large post-training NTK change. The authors call this delayed rich regime 'grokking' (Fig. 10, App. F.3). No test accuracy or generalization delay is measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer imbalance, combined with network shape, governs a delayed lazy-to-rich transition measured by change in the NTK.

fits_no_version.finding: In linear networks, NTK change (a lazy/rich indicator) depends on layer imbalance and weight-to-target ratio (Fig. 6). This is a regime measure, not delayed generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-to-target ratio and layer imbalance set lazy versus rich dynamics in linear networks.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025)
record.problems: The MNIST evidence is presented as accuracy curves without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The reported experiment uses one dataset and one MLP setup; it does not directly measure the proposed lazy-to-rich mechanism.

untested.parts: Text and molecule data. Weight-norm control as such (weight decay is fixed at 1e-4). Direct measurement of a lazy-to-rich transition in the MNIST MLP (no NTK or feature-change metric on MNIST). Dependence on training-set size.
No algorithmic-dataset experiment and no training-set-size sweep.
No test of efficiency, critical dataset size or ungrokking.
No comparison of algorithms across runs.
Adam is used throughout. Optimizer and numerical artifacts are not controlled or varied.

record.verdict_notes: Position paper. The only empirical grokking result is Fig. 8: one dataset, one architecture, curves only, no seeds or uncertainty. The setup closely follows Kumar et al. (2024) and Omnigrok's large-initialization MNIST result, so the evidence is a small replication. The cited claims about algorithmic tasks and Kunin et al. are not this study's results.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment on a small algorithmic dataset or training-set-size sweep; the cited algorithmic-task findings are not this study’s results.
No measurement of gradual formation of a generalizing circuit, removal of memorizing components, or progress measures anticipating a test-accuracy jump.

The experiment tests a four-layer tanh MLP on MNIST and varies initialization/scaling, but does not test other non-algorithmic modalities, weight-norm regularization itself, or directly measure the lazy-to-rich transition in the MNIST model.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning experiment on realistic data.

The paper discusses a weight-to-target account and tests scaling changes, but does not measure whether a more efficient generalizing circuit displaces memorization, or test a critical dataset size or ungrokking below it.
No comparison of algorithms learned across runs.
No controlled test of adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits as the cause of the delay.

relationships.condition: 4-layer tanh MLP, 1000 MNIST samples, Adam with weight decay 1e-4, MSE loss
relationships.reason: With 5× initialization the default run groks (r1). Lowering the weight-to-target ratio by weight, target, input or output scaling eliminates the delay (r2–r5). Figure-only, single run each.
relationships.display_finding: The baseline grokked with 5× initialization, while weight, target, input, or output scaling that lowered the weight-to-target ratio eliminated the delay.
